explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, "I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1), which means nothing he needs is missing. Picture a cookie jar that never runs empty. And notice the reason: it's all because "the LORD is my shepherd."

Earn is a fair guess, because most of us figure we have to work for what we need. But David points at the shepherd instead: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). The shepherd is the headline here, not David's paycheck. The word is "want," as in lacking something.

Lose sounds close, but David isn't talking about dropping something along the way. He says, "I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1), meaning he won't be missing what he needs. A sheep isn't out there patting its pockets. It has a shepherd.

That's it, friend. "He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters" (Psalm 23:2). Lying down, green grass, quiet water. Nobody in that picture is checking their phone or sprinting anywhere. It's the calmest scene you could ask for.

No hustle in this picture, friend. David says the LORD "makes me lie down in green pastures" (Psalm 23:2), and nobody lies down in the middle of a grind. Then "quiet waters" seals it. This is a scene for slowing down, not speeding up.

I get why you'd pick that, but read the scene again. David has "green pastures" and "quiet waters" (Psalm 23:2). Grass to lie in and calm water to drink. That's a peaceful spot, and nothing in these words is closing in.

Baked just right, baker. David says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). Restores is a caring word, the kind you use for something worn that gets set right again. The LORD looks after the grass and water, and He looks after David on the inside too.

Tests is an understandable guess, friend, since we all know that nervous feeling. But David says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). Restores is gentle. It's about putting something back to good shape, not grading it.

Weighs belongs on a kitchen scale, friend. I weigh flour all day, but David's word here is different: "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). Nobody is measuring his soul. It's being cared for and made whole.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, "He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). The reason he gives is the LORD's own name. So the guiding isn't a one-time favor. It's tied to who the LORD is.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: That one sounds sensible, since sheep make up a flock. But David's words are, "He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). The reason he names is the LORD's name. The flock doesn't appear in that line.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: Land is a good guess for a pasture song, friend. But David says the LORD guides him "in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). Land isn't mentioned in that line. The reason David gives is the LORD's name.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. David says, "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). I think this is a heavy line, and it's okay to let it be heavy. His reason isn't how brave he is. It's that the LORD is with him.

I understand the pull of that answer, friend. But look at how David says it: "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). He doesn't claim his own strength in that valley. The reason he gives is that the LORD is with him.

Nice try, friend, but David never says how long the valley is. He says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). That's his reason, and it stands even in a valley of the shadow of death. I think that's a comfort for anyone walking a hard road.
That's right, baker. David says, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). In a place that heavy, that's a quiet and steady line. Out there, the shepherd's tools bring comfort.
This one is true, friend, and here's the line: "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). It's said right in the valley of the shadow of death. David finds comfort there, not fear.

Box-worthy, baker. David says, "You prepare a table before me" (Psalm 23:5). That's a host getting things ready for a guest. Any baker knows the difference between getting a plate handed to you and having a whole spread set out just for you.
A tent is a decent guess for a shepherd's life, friend. But the line says, "You prepare a table before me" (Psalm 23:5). The picture is a host and a guest. David doesn't mention a tent here.

A bed would be cozy, friend, and David did talk about lying down back in verse 2. But this verse says, "You prepare a table before me" (Psalm 23:5). Now the picture is a host setting out a meal for a guest.

A quiet table far from trouble would be nice, but that's not what David says. He says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). The words are "in the presence of," not far away from. The table is set right where his enemies are around.
Right on, baker. David says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). Not far away. In their presence. That's quite a seat at the table, with the LORD as the host.

That's a keeper! David says, "my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5). A cup that spills over means there's more than it can hold. It's like a mixing bowl that fills right up past the rim. The LORD's care for David doesn't run short.

Spills do happen in my kitchen, friend, but that's not the picture here. David says, "You prepare a table before me" and "my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5). The LORD is the host, and the cup runs over because there's plenty. It's about abundance, not a mess.

No rush in this scene, friend. David says, "You prepare a table before me" and "my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5). A prepared table and a full cup say the host has taken care of everything. The overflowing cup says there's more than enough.

Fine work, baker! David says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). They're not out ahead of him or waiting at the end. They follow him, every day of his life. That's a lot of days with good company behind you.

Wealth and honor sound impressive, friend, but they're not on David's list. He says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). The two things following him are goodness and mercy, and they stay with him all his days.

Strength and wisdom are great things to ask for, friend. But David's line is, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). Those are the two that follow him, and the word is "all" the days.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Perfect bake! David ends with, "and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). Dwell means to stay, not to pass through. The song starts with a shepherd and finishes at home with Him, and the last word is "forever."

Hebron is a real place, friend, but David doesn't name it here. He ends with, "and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). His closing hope isn't a city. It's the LORD's house, for good.

Canaan is a good guess, since it's a land the Bible talks about. But David closes with, "and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). He doesn't name Canaan in this song. His last words are about the LORD's house, and the word is "forever."
